name: Gambits
goal: You can judge when a pawn offered in the opening is worth taking, and when to give one back to finish developing.

intro.text: A gambit offers a pawn, sometimes more, in return for time: quicker development, open lines or an attack. Before you take one, weigh the pawn against the moves it will cost you to win it and keep it. Some gambits only look like gifts: in the Queen's Gambit, Black can take the pawn on c4 but cannot keep it for long. In this Lesson you take a pawn that costs little, turn down one that costs too much, and let a pawn go when holding on to it would leave your pieces at home.

parts.title: The King's Gambit
parts.keyIdea: A pawn that costs you one move and leaves the enemy king less sheltered is worth taking; then develop rather than cling to it.
parts.text: From a game played on Lichess. You are Black. After 1.e4 e5, White has pushed the f-pawn two squares with 2.f4, the King's Gambit, and offers it to your e-pawn. Is the pawn worth taking?

credit.authors: Lichess; the players of the game

notes.text: 2...exf4 takes the pawn. It costs you only one move, and with White's f-pawn gone, the diagonal from a7 to g1 leads straight to White's king. The Engine prefers taking to turning the pawn down.

3.Nf3 developed a knight and stopped ...Qh4+. Instead of spending moves on keeping the f4 pawn, 3...d5 hits White's centre and opens a path for your bishop on c8. Holding the pawn with 3...g5 is also played, but it loosens your kingside pawns.
4.exd5 took your d-pawn. 4...Nf6 develops a knight that attacks d5 at once, so a piece, not your queen, will win the pawn back.

5.Bc4 defended the pawn, but your knight and your queen both attack d5 and only the bishop defends it, so 5...Nxd5 takes it. You are a pawn up again, your pieces are coming out, and White's king has no f-pawn to shelter it.

parts.title: The Vienna Gambit
parts.keyIdea: If taking a pawn lets your opponent chase your pieces back home, turn it down and strike in the centre instead.
parts.text: From a game played on Lichess. You are Black. After 1.e4 e5 2.Nc3 Nf6, White offers the f-pawn with 3.f4, the Vienna Gambit. This time, look at what taking it would cost you before you decide.

credit.authors: Lichess; the players of the game

notes.text: 3...d5 turns the pawn down and strikes at the centre. After 3...exf4 White would push 4.e5, and your knight on f6 would be driven back to g8: you would have an extra pawn, but White would have the centre and a lead in development. The Engine grades 3...exf4 as an inaccuracy.
4.fxe5 took your e-pawn, and 4...Nxe4 takes White's e-pawn in return. Material is level, and your knight sits on a strong central square, where it attacks White's knight on c3.
5.Nf3 developed. 5...Be7 brings out your bishop and gets you ready to castle. White's f-pawn has left its place in front of White's king, and you have given nothing away.

parts.title: The Budapest Gambit
parts.keyIdea: When your opponent is sure to win the pawn back, defend it with moves that develop, and let it go rather than spend more moves on it.
parts.text: From a game played on Lichess. You are White. After 1.d4 Nf6 2.c4, Black has pushed 2...e5, the Budapest Gambit, and offers the e-pawn. Decide whether to take it, and then how hard to fight to keep it.

credit.authors: Lichess; the players of the game

notes.text: 3.dxe5 takes the pawn. It costs you nothing, and now Black has to spend moves winning it back. The Engine prefers taking.
3...Ng4 attacked the pawn on e5. 4.Bf4 defends it and brings a bishop into play at the same time.
4...Nc6 attacked e5 a second time, and 5.Nf3 defends it a second time while it develops another piece.
5...Bb4+ checked your king. 6.Nbd2 blocks the check with a knight that comes into play, and your knight on f3 still guards e5.

6...Qe7 attacked e5 a third time, and you have only two defenders, so the pawn will go back to Black. Rather than spend more moves on it, 7.e3 opens the way for your bishop on f1 so you can castle soon. After 7...Ngxe5 8.Nxe5 Nxe5 material is level again, and the Engine prefers your position slightly.
